results.title: Blunt Cuts and Tonal Depth for Fine Hair Density
results.description: Thin hair presents a specific structural challenge: the low density of strands means that standard volume-building techniques often backfire, leaving the ends looking sparse rather than lush. For clients with this starting condition, the primary goal is not to add physical mass, which the hair cannot support, but to manage the visual weight and direction of the existing strands. The error most often cited by stylists is an excess of layering, a technique that works for thick, heavy hair by removing weight but destroys the perceived density of fine hair. When a stylist cuts too many distinct levels, the result is a jagged, see-through perimeter that highlights the lack of volume rather than creating it. The professional correction begins with a shift from discrete layers to continuous, blended shapes. Sam McKnight's approach to structure emphasizes how direction and texture create the finished shape; in this context, that means avoiding the "ruffled" look of over-thinning. Instead, stylists recommend a uniform, blunt cut. By keeping the bottom edge straight and heavy, the hair falls together, creating a solid line that tricks the eye into perceiving greater density. If movement is required, the technique shifts to "invisible" layers-long, graduated transitions that maintain the weight at the ends while adding lift at the crown. This creates volume where it is needed most without sacrificing the optical thickness of the perimeter. Shade and Surface Texture Color plays a critical role in how light interacts with the hair shaft, a factor Tracey Cunningham identifies as the limiting variable in any coloring result. A single, flat shade offers no depth, allowing the eye to see through the thin sections of hair. Conversely, contrasting tonal depth-alternating slightly darker and lighter pieces-interrupts the visual line of the strand. This contrast creates the illusion of shadow and dimension, making the mass of hair appear more substantial without changing its physical weight. The starting base color dictates how much contrast is visible; on very light or very dark bases, subtle variations may be lost, requiring more pronounced tonal shifts to achieve the same perceptual density.

GHOST RIDER Writer Wants Ryan Gosling's MCU Reboot to Go Full R-Rated Horror as Placeholder Synopsis Surfaces
results.description: Marvel Studios has big plans for Ryan Gosling as Ghost Rider, and comic book writer Benjamin Percy thinks the upcoming MCU reboot should take the character somewhere seriously dark. We're talking melting flesh, chains pulled from mouths, and enough supernatural horror to make this feel like a trip straight into Hell. Percy, who wrote Marvel's Ghost Rider comic series from 2022 to 2023, wants the new movie to embrace the character's darker side rather than follow the usual Marvel superhero formula. Speaking with ComicBook, Percy explained why he believes an R-rated approach would be the right move: “Let me say that as a horror head, this is my time, right? I’m in my zone right now. "I’m sure whatever Marvel conjures up is going to be great, but I would lean towards the R-rated horror version of the character and not do the standard cape and spandex, MCU type, which can be very effective if you’re doing a Doomsday storyline, or an X-Men storyline. “But in this case, I would really lean into, like, Johnny pulling hot chains out of his mouth, Hellraiser style, or his skin melting right off of him with a halo of flames around. Like, give us the body horror. Give us a really hellish iteration of Ghost Rider on the screen.” I'm on board with that approach! Ghost Rider is a flaming skeleton who makes deals with demons and savagely punishes the wicked. There's plenty of room to make an awesome supernatural horror movie here, especially if Marvel is willing to let the filmmakers get a little crazy with the character. While most MCU films stick with a PG-13 rating, the success of Deadpool and Wolverine proved that Marvel can deliver an R-rated comic book movie and still bring in a massive audience. An adult-oriented Ghost Rider movie could be a great way to explore the MCU's supernatural corner. Marvel officially announced Gosling's casting during its San Diego Comic-Con presentation in July. The actor will headline a solo Ghost Rider movie directed by Shawn Levy, whose credits include Deadpool & Wolverine and the upcoming Star Wars: Starfighter. The film is scheduled to arrive in theaters in 2028, with Starfighter screenwriter Jonathan Tropper handling the script. Heated Rivalry star Connor Storrie is also reportedly in talks to play the movie's villain, although details about the character remain under wraps. Gosling's Ghost Rider is also expected to have a role in Marvel's planned Midnight Sons movie, which would bring together some of the MCU's supernatural heroes. In addition to Percy's comments, a placeholder synopsis for the reboot has surfaced, and it offers an interesting possibility for the story. The description comes directly from Volume 10 of Marvel's Ghost Rider comic, so it shouldn't be treated as confirmation of the movie's plot. Still, it could offer a clue about the direction Marvel is considering. “Johnny Blaze has the perfect life: a wife and two kids, a job at an auto repair shop, and a small-town community that supports him… But Johnny isn’t doing well. He has nightmares of monsters when he sleeps. And he sees bloody visions when he’s awake. This life is beginning to feel like a prison. And there’s a spirit in him that’s begging to break out.” Gosling played a major role in getting the project off the ground. During a previously interview, Feige revealed that the actor was the one who developed the concept and convinced Levy to get involved. “It was Gosling who had the vision. It was Gosling who had the pitch that won over Shawn, that had them come and pitch us this idea, which led to us on stage today.” Gosling clearly passionate about the character, and the fact that he approached Marvel with a specific take tells us he completely invested in telling a great story that he’s excited about. Whether that vision matches Percy's desire for a full-on R-rated horror movie remains to be seen. Personally, I'd love to see Marvel embrace the frightening side of Ghost Rider. Give us the demonic imagery, the terrifying transformations, the hellfire, and the brutal consequences of being possessed by a supernatural force. The MCU has an opportunity to do something different with this character, and hopefully Gosling and Levy take full advantage of it. Would you rather see an R-rated Ghost Rider horror movie, or do you think Marvel can pull off the character with a PG-13 rating?
